articles.title_orig: United ‘hijack’ text scare forces plane to turn back
articles.title_zh: United ‘hijack’ text scare forces plane to turn back
articles.content_orig:
By ALYSSA GUZMAN, US NEWS REPORTER
Published: 12:22 EDT, 27 October 2026 | Updated: 12:35 EDT, 27 October 2026
A United Airlines flight attendant spotted terrifying texts allegedly sent by a passenger threatening to hijack the aircraft, forcing it to urgently return to Las Vegas.
Dante Milne, 25, of Wood-Ridge, New Jersey , was arrested in Las Vegas on Saturday after allegedly making threats while onboard United Flight 1681.
Milne was spotted by a flight attendant allegedly sending threats to hijack the Vegas-to-Newark plane, causing the United worker to report him and for the plane to return to Sin City, the complaint viewed by KSNV reportedly said.
He allegedly wrote to someone that he was 'gonna hijack this' plane and would 'crash ur [sic] row only.'
It is unclear how the message was transmitted or who the recipient was. The incident occurred roughly 13 minutes into the flight.
The flight attendant did not engage with Milne, but instead reported the scary messages to the cockpit. The pilot told air traffic controllers that the 'passenger does not know anything is going on,' recordings showed.
'No restraint. Passenger is compliant because he is unaware,' the pilot said.
Law enforcement met the plane, and Milne was taken into custody and booked into the Clark County Jail. He has since bailed out, court records showed.
Dante Milne, of Wood-Ridge, New Jersey, was arrested by federal authorities in Las Vegas on Saturday after messaging someone that he was going to 'hijack' the plane
Milne was spotted by a flight attendant, causing the United worker to report him to the cockpit  (stock image)
As part of his bail conditions, he was told to stay out of trouble, according to 8 News Now .
He has been charged with a felony for making a threat or false information in an act of terrorism.
Milne was taken into custody without incident, and all other passengers were evacuated. The plane was then thoroughly checked.
The 149 passengers then unfortunately had to wait overnight as the flight crew had exceeded their mandated operating hours. The flight departed on Sunday morning.
The Daily Mail has reached out to Milne and United for comment.
'Potential security concern': United flight makes U-turn after flight crew witness peculiar passenger behavior United passenger arrested for hijacking threat on Las Vegas-Newark flight The plane was headed from Las Vegas to Newark on Saturday when a flight attendant spotted what… pic.twitter.com/32YCJZ2Vlk
The flight had barely left the Harry Reid International Airport before having to return due to the messages. Milne faces a terrorism charge
The scare comes just days after another United Airlines flight experienced a huge bang during turbulence so severe that the plane began plunging, injuring four flight attendants.
Passengers said the turbulence felt like a sudden drop after hearing a 'huge bang,' with one witness reporting that one of the injured flight attendants had blood on their head and leg.
Medical personnel saw four flight attendants in total, including one who was transported to the hospital for further treatment, United told The Daily Mail in a statement.
United Airlines Flight 1157 had initially left Honolulu, Hawaii, before landing safely in Los Angeles, California.

articles.title_orig: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.title_zh: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.content_orig:
Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.
The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.
Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.
TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.
Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.
China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.
While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.
Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.

articles.title_orig: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, the offices of President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said. Their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole".
After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts.
Tuesday's 90-minute phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki, and showed "big differences in views", StÃ¸re said.
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
The call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security".
StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
He - like Stubb and StÃ¸re - had agreed to continue their direct phone communication, the statement added.
Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
StÃ¸re said all their allies had been informed of the call ahead of time.
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue, telling Danish broadcaster DR, it had not been "co-ordinated with any of the rest of us".
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates, was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US.
But last week, Stubb, StÃ¸re and Zelesnky met Witkoff in the Norwegian capital, before the US special envoy travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin.
Following the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months.
After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on November's trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security".
Stubb and StÃ¸re are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
As the US administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the European Union of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".

articles.title_orig: Israelis vote in a pivotal election centered on Netanyahu's leadership, Oct. 7 and its aftermath
articles.title_zh: Israelis vote in a pivotal election centered on Netanyahu's leadership, Oct. 7 and its aftermath
articles.content_orig:
Watch: What does Israel's election mean for Gaza - and the world
Turnout so far is at record levels, as Israelis vote in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.
Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is almost neck-and-neck with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot in the race to become prime minister.
But neither of their political blocs is projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a government - and weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.
The campaign has been shaped by the issues of democracy and security, and the election is widely being seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's rule.
Many leading parties complained on Tuesday morning of alleged irregularities at polling stations across the country - but Israel's Central Election Committee (CEC) says there is no evidence of systematic tampering with ballot slips.
Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.
Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties which have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.
Other leaders in the bloc include former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.
For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a new term will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history .
Polling published on Friday suggests Gadi Eisenkot (left) is in a tight race with incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu (right)
There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers . However, all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
The campaign has been dominated by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.
They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.
They also point to what they see as threats to democracy under Netanyahu, who faces an ongoing trial on corruption charges - which he denies - and is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before the 7 October attacks.
Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.
On Sunday, Israel's Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had pushed for last-minute military action that could trigger a confrontation with Iran prior to the elections, but was opposed by his own military chief Eyal Zamir. The following day, CNN reported that he had also tried to persuade Trump to carry out new strikes on Iran, but the US leader had refused to give the green light. Netanyahu denied both reports.
He also made headlines in the final days of his campaign for posting an AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb hitting Tel Aviv, warning that he is the only leader who can protect Israel "if the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons". Eisenkot called him "hysterical".
Another dominating issue has been conscription, with Netanyahu's government failing to enforce a Supreme Court ruling that ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study should be conscripted to the military - a highly divisive move .
Netanyahu is currently in coalition with two ultra-Orthodox parties, which have supported protests against conscription
Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on the Gaza Strip, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means.
Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.
Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.
The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics.
Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.
Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex, but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in.
Far-right ministers and settlers Itamar Ben Gvir (left) and Bezalel Smotrich (centre) and have been key voices in Netanyahu's government, and lead separate far-right parties
An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while hundreds of thousands are casting ballots for the first time.
At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly.
Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.
Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists are also casting ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties which are thought to have strong support from that demographic.
Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.
An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title_orig: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.title_zh: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.content_orig:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: Skeleton of newly-discovered Nanotyrannus auctioned for $47.3m in New York
articles.title_zh: Skeleton of newly-discovered Nanotyrannus auctioned for $47.3m in New York
articles.content_orig:
The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has just been sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (Â£35.5m).
Nicknamed "Jodi", the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton was auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.
The Late Cretaceous carnivore was expected to fetch at least $9m when it went under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed "Gus", for a record $50.1m in July.
The sale comes amid debate in the scientific community over whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately or displayed publicly.
Sotheby's described "Jodi" as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".
The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science". The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.
The identify of the buyer, who won after a thrilling 12 minutes of auction bidding between six interested parties, has not been disclosed.
It becomes the second-most valuable dinosaur fossil ever sold, behind "Gus". The third-most valuable was a Stegosaurus dubbed "Apex" which was sold by Sotheby's in July 2024 for $44.6m.
Megan Jenkins, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".
"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jenkins said.
Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.
"Jodi" was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.
The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hell Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.
Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from "Jodi" in 2006.
The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.
The auction of "Jodi" comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.
Researchers told the BBC after the sale of "Gus" that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.
Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".
"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."
He said at the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.
Responding to Tuesday's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that "Jodi" could disappear from public view.
"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.
But Jenkins told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.
"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

articles.title_orig: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.title_zh: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.content_orig:
New Delhi, India – India’s armed forces are locked in multiple ongoing face-offs with the Chinese army along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the chief of India’s paramilitary border force guarding the Himalayan frontier with China has said.
The remarks late last week by Shatrujeet Kapur, the director-general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) paramilitary force, come nearly four months after local civil society groups in the remote northeastern region told Al Jazeera that Chinese forces were increasingly encroaching on Indian territory and denying Indian troops access to patrolling points, angering locals.
Chinese President Xi Jinping was in New Delhi last month – his first trip to India in seven years – for the BRICS summit, where he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines, as the two capitals pursued a cautious thaw in bilateral ties. That thaw is partly driven by United States President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has pushed nuclear-armed rivals Beijing and New Delhi closer.
Yet the alleged Chinese incursions into India underscore how, despite warm handshakes in New Delhi, tensions along the 3,500-kilometre (2,200-mile) border between the neighbours threaten to undercut efforts to normalise ties.
They also pose a major political challenge to Modi, who has built an image as being strong on national security, but who has in recent years faced difficult questions about the relationship with China.
The face-offs with Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh – that “still continue”, according to Kapur – come six years after at least 20 Indian troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat with Chinese forces in mountainous Ladakh.
Though satellite imagery and multiple accounts, including from within the Indian security establishment, have since pointed to China effectively taking control of parts of previously disputed territory since that fight, the Modi government has refused to concede that it has given up any land.
And five days after Kapur’s comments on recent standoffs, the Indian government is yet to confirm the nature of the border tensions, instead offering more boilerplate criticisms of China.
Kapur, the ITBP chief, was speaking at a felicitation ceremony for the paramilitary force’s personnel, where he revealed that commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the border with China.
Arunachal Pradesh’s remote Upper Subansiri region – where the ongoing face-offs are reported – had seen the first clash between independent India and China in August 1959, which killed at least two Indian soldiers.
Then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of the remoteness of the region in his account of the clash, when he told Parliament that the border post under Chinese attack was roughly three weeks’ march from the nearest roadhead.
The decades-long India-China border dispute is rooted in a British-drawn border, called the McMahon Line. In 1914, British India and Tibet, not under Chinese control at the time, signed the Simla Convention, demarcating their border. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has treated the McMahon Line as its border with China. But China, which came under communist rule in 1949, rejects the line as the boundary with India, arguing that Tibet lacked the authority to conclude the agreement independently.
Beijing claims the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh and refers to it as “South Tibet” or “Zangnan”. China also controls Aksai Chin, a slice of the disputed Kashmir region that India and Pakistan claim in full.
With their territorial claims unresolved, India and China signed an agreement in 1993 to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), their de facto boundary from 1962, pending a final border settlement. They continue to disagree over its precise alignment.
Those differences were never bridged in the following years, keeping the disputed frontier a persistent flashpoint in relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
The dispute erupted again into a deadly confrontation in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh, with both sides accusing the other of crossing the LAC. At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed, and China later acknowledged four deaths among its troops.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, said that border tensions amid a thaw in bilateral relations now appear as “part of a pattern” – “likely a pressure tactic by Beijing,” he added.
And due to the undemarcated border, “stand-offs are bound to occur from time to time, some of which may go out of hand”, Donthi warned.
But the 2020 clash also pushed Modi into a corner domestically, as the opposition parties pressured the government over its opaque handling of China. The Modi government also faced opposition complaints over restrictions on parliamentary scrutiny, questions about whether intelligence agencies had detected the Chinese troop build-up, and limited disclosure of operational details.
Contradictions between the government’s own stand and Modi’s claims also prompted accusations that he was trying to minimise – or even hide – the scale of the crisis along the border.
On June 17, 2020, soon after the Galwan clash, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar spoke to his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
“The Chinese side sought to erect a structure in Galwan Valley on our side of the LAC,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said after the phone call. “While this became a source of dispute, the Chinese side took premeditated and planned action that was directly responsible for the resulting violence and casualties. It reflected an intent to change the facts on ground in violation of all our agreements to not change the status quo.”
Yet two days later, Modi said on Twitter, now X, that “neither has anyone been able to enter our territory, nor is anyone still on our territory” – an assertion that disputed the foreign ministry’s account. If no Chinese troops had crossed the LAC, why had Indian soldiers been forced to fight them, the opposition and other strategic analysts asked?
The government has never answered those questions, with Modi’s office only issuing a clarification that the prime minister meant that there were no Chinese troops still in Indian territory after the clash.
Six years since the Ladakh clash, the Chinese incursion has returned to challenge Modi’s strongman image at home – which has already taken a hit from youth-led protests in the country that forced out Modi’s education minister in July this year.
In his address, ITBP chief Kapur also recalled the 2020 clash, outlining a specialised training programme “to better equip personnel to deal with” a Ladakh-like situation.
Kapur, who is due to retire this week, also warned that China’s frontier military capabilities had advanced – and Indian forces may not be able to take a fight head-on by traditional methods.
The Crisis Group’s Donthi said that the Modi government “presents an image of a hard security state with zero tolerance for national security failures”. but “the power differential with China is quite sharp, so it tends to downplay any event that reflects poorly”.
The opposition Congress party’s top leader in Arunachal Pradesh state, Bosiram Siram, said that Chinese troops have intruded nearly 50km (31 miles) deep into Indian territory in remote Upper Subansiri.
A Siram-led party delegation visited border areas in August after initial reports of China’s incursions, and Siram added that “Chinese personnel are stationed up there”, referring to Indian territory.
“You can see the [Chinese] Army. They are on top of the mountains, while we are down below,” Siram added.
In response to the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that “the situation in India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”. He did not comment on

articles.title_orig: Mbappe seeks to defuse China anger after 'ill-judged' Mao comments
articles.title_zh: Mbappe seeks to defuse China anger after 'ill-judged' Mao comments
articles.content_orig:
A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over MbappÃ©'s comments on a "Chinese dictator"
Kylian MbappÃ© has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.
MbappÃ© had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,"  MbappÃ© said in a statement.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian MbappÃ©'s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like MbappÃ©.
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's AurÃ©lien TchouamÃ©ni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, MbappÃ© does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.
Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao
Chinese fans have been criticising MbappÃ© â who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements â of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another  comment on Weibo.
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
MbappÃ© has a significant commercial presence in China
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with MbappÃ©, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on MbappÃ©, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with MbappÃ©" topping the list.
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.
MbappÃ© has said some of the memes "reveal a lack of political and human awareness"
It's unclear when the MbappÃ© meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.
MbappÃ© is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling MbappÃ© Mobut â a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.
In an interview with France Football in September, MbappÃ© acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."
Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

articles.title_orig: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry
articles.title_zh: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday.
President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.
"That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.
Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.
Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.
Trump negotiated USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."
Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.
She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.
"Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."
Honda is the s econd-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor , but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.
While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants.
"I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.
The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

articles.title_orig: A wounded Ukrainian soldier waited 2 days to be rescued. Then a drone flew him to safety
articles.title_zh: A wounded Ukrainian soldier waited 2 days to be rescued. Then a drone flew him to safety
articles.content_orig:
Kostiantyn Vlasenko was huddled in a hole under the boiler of a bombed-out school when he came to a terrifying conclusion: To survive, he needed to amputate his only remaining foot.
The Ukrainian infantryman had already lost his left foot in a Russian drone strike in February. His right leg was broken and bent in the same attack, hindering his ability even to crawl. About three months later, after working up the courage, he grabbed his knife, sliced off his foot and applied a tourniquet to staunch the bleeding.
On October 4, after almost eight months holed up in the boilerhouse - and 491 days on Ukraineâs drone-infested frontlines - the 49-year-old was rescued in dramatic fashion: A giant, six-propellor drone, controlled remotely, whisked a harnessed and dangling Vlasenko high into the sky and spirited him 15 km (9 miles) away to safety.
The operation was the first known aerial drone rescue of a soldier, Ukrainian commanders said, in a five-year conflict that has seen the technology used with unprecedented scale and lethality, redefining modern warfare.

A six-rotor drone hovers in a pale blue sky with a black arrow pointing right to show its direction of travel. Its battery and electric winch are labeled on the central frame. Below it, Kostiantyn Vlasenko hangs in a yellow harness, with a circled detail highlighting that both of his feet are missing after a Russian drone attack. Callouts explain that an earlier drone delivery brought him the harness, and that three Vampire drones escorted the rescue drone to distract Russian drones. Smaller escort drones appear in the background and at the bottom of the image.
The infantryman endured one of the longest Ukrainian deployments on record along the front lines of the conflict against Russia. The area is known as the kill zone because of the vast armies of drones swarming the skies which make any movement potentially fatal. Nowhere is safe.
Soldiers on both sides are forced to dig foxholes deep underground and often find themselves trapped in their positions for many months. Casualties remain high, though the primacy of drones has largely halted Russian advances.
The drone rescue marked a stunning turnaround for Vlasenko, who had largely written off his chances in the agonizing months after amputating his own limb.
âI had already buried myself,â the soldier told Reuters from his hospital bed in the northeastern city of Kharkiv as he looked down at his two bandaged stumps. âI knew there was no hope left.â
Vlasenkoâs story of his ordeal and rescue was corroborated by the Ukrainian military and video footage from a camera mounted on the drone that saved him, although Reuters could not independently verify all elements of his account.
Vlasenko serves in the 30th Mechanized Brigade deployed in the Kharkiv region. In May last year, he was sent to a frontline position to join a comrade, whose call sign was Basky.
The men, jammed in a cramped dugout, were supplied by daily drone supply drops, including chocolate and premium cigarettes on Vlasenkoâs birthday.
When it was finally time to rotate troops in autumn last year, two relief soldiers were both killed on their way to Vlasenkoâs position, he said. Two more soldiers sent to retrieve their bodies were also killed.
âThatâs when I remember realizing that this would definitely be a turning point,â said the married infantryman. âThat no one would get out anymore.â
After 10 months together, Vlasenko and Basky were eventually forced to abandon their position in mid-February when their foxhole flooded, forcing them to take refuge in a ruined school building. The respite proved short-lived. A Russian surveillance drone soon spotted them emerging to pick up a package of dry clothing and food dropped by comrades.
Another Russian drone bombed them, killing Basky on his 50th birthday. Vlasenkoâs left foot was ripped apart by the blast. He seriously injured his other leg as he fell.
Barely able to move, he found shelter in a pit, about 80 by 60 centimetres wide, that he found beneath the metal boiler that once heated the school.
His left foot gradually ârotted awayâ, said Vlasenko, who found the memory painful to discuss. The right lower leg was so badly injured, with the bone protruding, that he eventually decided to sever the foot.
âI had to amputate it because it was just dragging along behind me,â he said. âThe leg was dragging so much that the bone was sticking out further and further.â
âSo I no longer had either of my legs.â
Vlasenko is recovering in hospital in the city of Kharkiv after his ordeal ended this month. REUTERS/Sofiia Gatilova
As Vlasenko started losing hope, his commanders further back from the front lines worked with the 92nd Assault Brigade and other units on ways to get him out.
Evacuations of the wounded from the kill zone by pickup trucks or armoured vehicles had proved almost impossible because of the aerial-drone threat, according to the officer in charge of the operationâs planning, who introduced himself only by his call sign Alex.Â Â Â Â
Ukrainian units had started using unmanned ground vehicles on wheels or tracks, but this was also risky, he added. Two such vehicles attempted to reach Vlasenko. Both were destroyed by Russian drones.
Rescue seemed impossible, the officer said.
Then officers heard about a new heavy-lift drone being made by a local manufacturer, Gurzuf Defence. With its six vertical rotors and black skeleton, it resembles a huge insect â and can lift up to 90 kg for up to 25 km.
It would need to fly Vlasenko â who the officers reckoned weighed about 70 kg after more than a year on the front â for 15 km to a safe position further back from the front.
The mission was fraught with danger: Larger Ukrainian aerial drones are often intercepted by smaller Russian first-person-view drones, which allow the remote pilot to see the scene from the craftâs perspective in real time.
In early October, Vlasenko found that one of his regular supply parcel drops contained unexpected items: a strange harness and a phone with instruction videos saved.
Vlasenko secured himself in the triangle and clipped it to a carabiner Â hanging from the droneâs winch.

articles.title_orig: A 'never-ending' cruise has halted operations and told residents to disembark in Cambodia after fuel costs rose over 300%
articles.title_zh: A 'never-ending' cruise has halted operations and told residents to disembark in Cambodia after fuel costs rose over 300%
articles.content_orig:
A cruise ship selling the promise of a permanent life at sea has come to an abrupt stop.
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey , announced on Tuesday that it had suspended operations in Cambodia amid steep increases in fuel costs.
The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
The US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, and Iran's subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a vital chokepoint for global oil shipments — sent energy prices soaring around the world.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
Villa Vie Residences sold permanent cabins on its 509-cabin ship, the Odyssey, ranging from $119,999 to $439,999. Its pitch to residents was a never-ending cruise around the world with stops at more than 400 ports of call and a global circumnavigation every three-and-a-half years.
The ship, which has a pool deck, spa, and a pickleball court, also offered five-year residencies, starting at $59,999.
The rising fuel costs put the company's operating model under unsustainable financial pressure, Villa Vie Residences said. The company added that it was evaluating options, but that no financing or transaction had been finalized.

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," the company said. "Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured."
The press release said the company was working with residents to coordinate disembarkation in Cambodia and to identify temporary living arrangements for them.
The Odyssey first set sail from Belfast in September 2024 after four months of delays.
Villa Vie Residences did not say how many residents were affected and did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

articles.title_orig: Boeing share price plummets with slower 737 production and free cash flow growth outlook
articles.title_zh: Boeing share price plummets with slower 737 production and free cash flow growth outlook
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock was down about 9% during the call.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Meta director Rohit Patel departs after 8 years to take on Microsoft Office Suite
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Meta director Rohit Patel departs after 8 years to take on Microsoft Office Suite
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc , a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.
Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan , AI researcher Andrew Tulloch , and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith .
Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.
Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.
The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents.
“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”
In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.
Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models.
“I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.”
Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.
His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.”
Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.”
Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.
OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta , SpaceXAI , and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.
Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.
“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”
There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.
“My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.”
Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.
As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.
For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.
“Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.”

articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) - Gold prices are trading at session highs after the latest data showed an improving picture of the attitudes of U.S. consumers this month.
The Consumer Confidence Index rose to 91.7 in October, above economists’ consensus forecast for an 81 reading and also above the upwardly revised 84.2 print from September, the Conference Board announced on Tuesday.
The Present Situation Index—based on consumers' assessment of current business and labor market conditions—increased by 8.6 points to 120.4. The Expectations Index—based on consumers' short-term outlook for income, business, and labor market conditions—recovered by 6.9 points to 72.6, only partially reversing three consecutive monthly declines. The survey period for this month's preliminary results was October 1 - 21.
Gold prices were setting fresh session highs in the wake of the 10 am ET data release, with spot gold last trading at $4,048.48 per ounce at the time of writing for a gain of 0.78% on the daily chart.
“Consumer confidence advanced in October, driven primarily by improved perceptions of current and expected business conditions,” said Fergus McCormick, Senior Economist, Global Indicators at The Conference Board. “The recovery was in line with retail gasoline prices easing from September to October. Yet, despite the increase in October, consumer confidence remained on the long-term downward trend that's persisted over the past few years. Consumers planned less spending on services and durable goods over the next six months. This likely reflected higher price levels and persistent inflation, which eroded consumers' purchasing power.”
“Among write-in responses in October, consumers continued to express frustration with rising costs,” he added. “References to prices, the high cost of food and groceries, and oil and diesel prices rose. Comments about war and conflict eased for a second straight month but remained elevated. Mentions of jobs and employment as an area of concern also ticked up, though to a lesser extent.”
“On a six-month moving average basis, only consumers under age 35 and those with a household income of $100k or more expressed an increase in confidence,” the report noted. “By generation, confidence amongst Gen X, Baby Boomers, and the Silent Generation continued to trail significantly behind Gen Z and Millennials, widening a sharp generational divide that has emerged over the past two years. In October, confidence improved across all political affiliations—but much more so for Republicans.”
Consumers' average 12-month inflation expectations declined in October but remained elevated at 5.8%,” the Conference Board said. “Consumers still expected higher interest rates over the next 12 months. Overall, more consumers in October expected stock prices to increase rather than decrease in the next 12 months.”
Jeffrey Roach, Chief Economist at LPL Financial, noted that business conditions and discretionary spending both improved in October.
"Business conditions are the best since April when consensus believed the war with Iran would be short-lived, inflation was less sticky, and the AI-trade dominated headlines," he said. "Even more noteworthy, the top five spending plans included restaurants and movies. Several discretionary sectors are vibrant, although consumers said they will cut back on hotels and airfare."
Roach pointed out that employment opportunities also appeared more plentiful, and home buying plans improved for the third consecutive month.
"Consumers may be tightening their belts, but some experiences are still a priority," he said. "Given the other data on core capital shipments, auto sales, and broader consumer spending, Q3 economic growth will likely be above 3% as the economy plows ahead, elevating annual growth to 2.2% for the full year."

articles.title_orig: AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
articles.title_zh: AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has announced that its AI models have made several scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics.
The AI giant said on Monday that the three new discoveries concerned the fields of harmonic analysis, complexity theory and quantum field theory.
Among the discoveries, AI models proved the local smoothing conjecture, one of the central propositions of harmonic analysis, in every spatial dimension for the first time, according to OpenAI.
Researchers in harmonic analysis, a branch of mathematics that studies how complex signals and functions can be broken down into elementary waves, had previously only proved the theory in three dimensions.
Alex Iosevich, a professor of mathematics at the University of Rochester who specialises in harmonic analysis, said OpenAI appeared to have “cracked” the conjecture in a “historic development”.
“The conjecture was formulated by my PhD adviser, Chris Sogge, so it is near and dear to my heart, and the news was a shock at first,” Iosevich told Al Jazeera.
“Now I am filled with joy and optimism, because the scientific enterprise as a whole is going to make giant leaps as a result of the AI revolution, and we have the chance to be a part of this historic development.”
Iosevich said he expected the field of theoretical mathematics to “change drastically” due to AI.
“I feel a twinge of sadness as a result,” Iosevich said.
“Many theoretical mathematicians I know feel the same way, but I firmly believe that these feelings will soon give way to the realisation that there is so much we can now accomplish.”
“Problems in pure mathematics did not arise in a vacuum,” he added. “Many of them came out of concrete physical considerations, and these connections can now be explored rapidly and decisively.”
According to OpenAI’s announcement, its models also disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which relates to the time it takes to solve complex computational problems, and provided “mathematically rigorous” proof of quantum chromodynamics, which studies the interaction of quarks and gluons.
Ryan Williams, an expert in computational complexity theory at MIT, said a confirmed refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis would be a major development.
“The ETH has been widely believed true since the late 1990s and a great deal of theoretical computer science was built on it being true,” Williams told Al Jazeera.
“We are working to verify and examine their proof and determine if it holds up,” Williams said.
“Their proof proposes a mysterious new method to more efficiently solve a variety of fundamental problems that have a wide range of potential applications.”
Williams said that while the development would not have real-world applications in the short-term, it could potentially lead to many “future real-world benefits for society”.
“It is hard to predict what will be possible next, because it’s a shocking development,” he said.
The ChatGPT creator said it had reached out to scientists outside the company to turn its “raw research data into scientific understanding”.
The San Francisco-based company said it decided on several different methods for releasing the findings based on consultations with three expert groups chosen to act as “shepherds”.
While the groups collaborating on the mathematics and computer science problems opted to make the AI-produced data public immediately, the physics group decided to defer the release in order to write up their own interpretation of the findings, OpenAI said.
“All of these approaches involve tradeoffs,” OpenAI said.
“On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community,” the $852bn start-up said.
“On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.”
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.
Last month, Claude creator Anthropic announced the discovery of a new enzyme said to resemble CRISPR , the groundbreaking gene editing mechanism used in treating conditions such as cancer and sickle cell disease.
Anthropic’s announcement drew mixed reactions among scientists.
While some researchers hailed the finding as an exciting development, others suggested that the AI company had exaggerated its significance.

articles.title_zh: Ford Fathom will be the cheapest American EV capable of powering a house
articles.content_orig:

Ford announced two new EV chargers today that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid.
The new chargers promise to be about half the cost of Ford’s existing equivalent products , which could make the technology available to more households. Ford said the Fathom itself will start at $28,350.
The Fathom will be capable of delivering “over 10 kW” to a home, Ford said. That would allow the electric vehicle to substitute for a small standby generator. For most U.S. homes, it wouldn’t be enough to power everything, but it could keep a refrigerator and air conditioner operational for about half a day.
Such capability has been touted as an advantage EVs have over fossil fuel vehicles, but not many EVs come properly equipped, and the chargers required to make use of vehicle-to-everything (V2X) services tend to be costly.
Ford’s two devices offer similar but differing capabilities.
The Home Power Station device can help customers shave their utility bill by charging the Fathom when power prices are low and sending electricity back to the home when prices are high. The automaker says it will cost around $650, about 50% less than its first-generation bidirectional charger.
The other option, Home Backup Power, is a package that bundles the Home Power Station with a second device, the Home Backup Panel, to allow the Fathom to also power parts or all of a home when the power goes out. Ford says the package will cost around $2,100, about 60% less than its first-generation product.
None of those prices include installation, which for existing V2X chargers can run up to $10,000, depending on how much electrical work needs to be done to prepare the home. Ford did not announce any partnerships with installers, though a spokesperson told TechCrunch that Ford would release more details at a later date.
Which loads the Fathom can power will vary by household and the specifics of each installation. Things like air conditioners and refrigerators, for example, typically require a large surge of power to start up, after which point their load drops. So-called soft-start devices can help mitigate the surge, though they add cost to the installation.
Both chargers will allow Fathom customers to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs), which use software to control a fleet of distributed energy storage devices, such as EVs.
As strain on the grid grows due to AI data centers, utilities have been exploring whether VPPs can help alleviate congestion at the edges.
Fathom owners who enroll and keep their truck plugged in can sell electricity back to the grid, often at a premium. Ford did not say how much Fathom owners can stand to make, but the payouts can be upwards of $1,000 per year, depending on the grid’s needs and the level of participation.
Automakers, including Ford , have been diving deep into energy storage as demand for such services surges. The Fathom-powered VPP is Ford’s latest foray into the market, but it’s unlikely to be its last.

articles.title_orig: UPS Earnings Deliver Good News for the U.S. Economy
articles.title_zh: UPS Earnings Deliver Good News for the U.S. Economy
articles.content_orig:
United Parcel Service on Tuesday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year guidance.
The guidance raise comes after the company already upped its outlook last quarter . UPS now said it's projecting full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion, as well as fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion.
Shares of UPS rose slightly in morning trading.
Here's how the company performed in its third quarter, compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter ended Sept. 30, UPS reported net income of $1.16 billion, or $1.37 per share, down slightly from net income of $1.31 billion, or $1.55, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time expenses, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.69. Revenue rose 6.7% to $22.9 billion.
In its domestic segment, the company said it saw a 4.5% increase in revenue, while its international segment had a 7.1% rise in revenue. Its supply chain solutions business saw an 18.2% revenue increase, which UPS said was primarily driven to growth in forwarding and logistics, including healthcare . On a call with analysts, CEO Carol Tomé said healthcare revenue exceeded $3 billion for the third consecutive quarter.
The company had previously said it expected its third-quarter domestic revenue to be flat and for domestic average daily volume to fall due to seasonal declines and the glide down with Amazon .
"We're driving more premium growth, improving revenue quality and mix, and creating greater operating leverage through a more efficient network," Tomé said on the call. "All of this is strengthening the underlying performance of our business."
UPS has been in the midst of a turnaround under Tomé's leadership, working to create a leaner business model and leveraging automation to position the company for growth.
As the company prepares for its peak holiday season, Tomé said the consumer remains resilient, and the growth in average daily volume between the third and fourth quarters will be consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume is expected to fall due to the reduction with Amazon.
She added that nearly 70% of all packages will flow through an automated process this holiday season.
